opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to the willingness to care about the details more than anyone around you would consider reasonable. You see this in sport. I fenced fairly seriously growing up, and the people who got really good weren't necessarily the most naturally gifted. They were the ones who'd go home and think about why a particular parry failed, and then drill it a few hundred more times until it was just in their body.

What surprised me was how directly that carried over into research and engineering. There's this mental model where world-class people are just smarter. Sometimes that's true. But more often they've built up a huge number of reps and really good taste about where to spend their effort. In ML, a lot of the progress comes from people who are relentless about running the experiment, actually looking at the results, and asking "wait, why did that happen?" instead of hand-waving past it.

The other piece is agency. Nobody hands you the path. A lot of people wait for permission or for someone to tell them what the important problem is. The people who get really good tend to just pick something hard, go deep on it, and put their work out into the world where people can see it. That's what creates the luck. Someone notices, you get pulled into a bigger problem, and the cycle compounds.

So if I had to compress it, I'd say: an almost unreasonable obsession with the craft, a fast feedback loop so you're actually learning from those reps, and the agency to go after the thing rather than waiting for it to come to you.

r001.rationale: The response describes repeated practice and compounding progress, but does not claim that becoming world-class can happen surprisingly quickly.

r002.rationale: It praises unusual dedication and effort, but does not say most people put in limited effort or that this explains rapid progress toward world-class performance.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that a lot of it is less about raw talent than people assume, and more about two things: the number of serious attempts you get, and how fast you learn from each one.

If you look at the people I've seen become genuinely world-class, whether in research or anything else, the common thread is that they compress their feedback loops. They do the thing, they look hard at what went wrong, and they go again, and they do that far more times than everyone around them. Over a year that compounds into a gap that looks like magic from the outside, but it's really just iteration count times learning rate.

The other piece is that you have to actually be in the arena. There's a huge difference between reading about something and sitting with the problem at eleven at night when the experiment fails and you have to figure out why. A lot of what looks like intuition in senior people is just scar tissue from hundreds of those nights. You can't shortcut it by reading more papers.

And then I think there's a thing about agency. The people who get really good are usually the ones who stop waiting for permission. They don't wait to be assigned the interesting problem, they go find it, they go find the person who knows the most about it, and they ask the dumb question. Being willing to look slightly foolish early on is a massive advantage, because the cost of looking foolish is small and the cost of staying ignorant is enormous.

So if I had to boil it down: pick something you genuinely care about, get your hands dirty as early as possible, maximize the number of real reps, and be ruthless about extracting the lesson from each one. Most people never get past the first step, and of those who do, most quit before the compounding kicks in.

r001.rationale: The response says repeated attempts compound into a gap over a year, but does not claim that reaching world-class performance itself can happen surprisingly quickly.

r002.rationale: It says world-class people make far more serious attempts than those around them and that most people quit before the compounding begins, linking others’ limited effort to faster progress through unusually many repetitions.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of it is finding something where you enjoy the process enough to spend an unreasonable amount of time doing it. You can want to be world-class, but that desire doesn’t necessarily get you through years of being mediocre and confronting what you don’t understand.

Then you need a really good feedback loop. You try something, you find out whether it worked, and you actually change your approach. It’s easy to accumulate experience without getting much better if you keep doing the things you’re already comfortable with.

Being around excellent people helps enormously, because they reveal how much better you could be. You watch someone solve a problem and realize, “Oh, they’re asking a question I wouldn’t even have thought to ask.” Suddenly you have something concrete to work on.

So I’d worry less initially about whether I had exceptional talent, and more about whether I’d found a pursuit where I was curious enough to keep pushing, with people and problems that would keep me honest.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes sustained effort over years but does not claim that reaching world-class performance can happen surprisingly quickly.

r002.rationale: The candidate recommends spending substantial time and using feedback, but does not attribute rapid progress to most people’s limited effort.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it is finding a feedback loop that lets you improve much faster than other people. You need to do the thing, notice precisely where you’re falling short, and then change how you do it. That sounds obvious, but you can spend years working hard without really doing that.

And taste matters a lot. Can you recognize what excellent work looks like? Can you look at something you’ve made and say, “This part is actually bad,” even though you put a huge amount of effort into it? Being around people who are much better than you helps because they make those distinctions visible.

Then there’s choosing something you find sufficiently interesting that you keep going when progress gets frustrating. Ambition can get you started, but curiosity makes the day-to-day work sustainable. You want to understand why something didn’t work badly enough that you’ll try again.

r001.rationale: The response says a good feedback loop can help you improve faster than other people, but does not claim that reaching world-class performance can happen surprisingly quickly.

r002.rationale: The response does not cite most people’s limited effort or unusually intense work as a cause of rapid progress. It says hard work can go on for years without effective feedback.
